title: Queues and linked lists
kicker: ENCT 252 · Data Structure and Algorithms · Chapters 3–4
subtitle: First in, first out; and a chain of nodes that grows one link at a time.

sections.title: The queue ADT
sections.body: A queue adds at the rear (enqueue) and removes from the front (dequeue): first in, first out. Think of a print queue. A plain array queue wastes space as the front creeps forward; a circular queue wraps the indices with modulo, so the array is fully reused. A deque allows both ends; a priority queue removes the highest-priority item first (implemented by a heap).

questions.prompt: Enqueue 1, 2, 3 then dequeue once. What is at the front?

figures.caption: Figure 3.1.1 — The queue ADT
figures.note: The same four numbers as the stack — now in arrival order.

sections.title: Circular queue arithmetic
sections.body: With array size N, advance an index by i = (i + 1) % N. The queue is empty when front == rear and (keeping one slot unused) full when (rear + 1) % N == front. Otherwise empty and full look identical.

worked.why: N = 5, front = 3, rear = 4. Enqueue one item.
Full check: (rear+1) mod N = 1 ≠ front 3, so there is still room.

questions.prompt: Why do circular queues usually leave one slot unused?

choices.text: To tell a full queue apart from an empty one (front == rear in both cases otherwise).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The sacrificed slot makes the two conditions different.

sections.title: The linked list
sections.body: A linked list stores each item in a node with a next pointer; you hold only the head. Insert at the head is O(1); insert after a known node is O(1); search is O(n); there is no index access. Nodes are allocated individually, so the list grows without a fixed size. Doubly linked nodes add a prev pointer (traverse both ways; deletion given the node is O(1)); circular lists link the last node back to the first.

questions.prompt: Cost of inserting at the head of a singly linked list?

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: That is inserting at the tail without a tail pointer.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Create a node, point it at the old head, move the head — no shifting.

figures.caption: Figure 4.1.1 — The linked list
figures.note: Inserting at the head reverses the order; watch the pointer arrows.

sections.title: Insert, delete and reverse
sections.body: To delete the node after p: q = p->next; p->next = q->next; delete q;. To reverse: keep prev, cur, next; for each node save next, point cur->next at prev, then advance all three. Always handle the empty list and the single-node case.

questions.prompt: To delete the node after p you must…

choices.text: Re-link p->next past it (and free it).

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: p would keep pointing at freed memory.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Otherwise the chain is broken or memory leaks.

figures.caption: Figure 4.2.1 — walking a list

sections.title: Applications: stack, queue and polynomials
sections.body: A list makes a stack (push/pop at the head) and a queue (insert at tail, remove at head, with a tail pointer) without a size limit. A polynomial is stored as a list of (coefficient, exponent) nodes in decreasing exponent; adding two polynomials walks both lists like merging sorted lists.

worked.why: Merge by exponent: x² terms add; x term alone; constants add.

questions.prompt: Why is a linked list good for sparse polynomials like x¹⁰⁰ + 1?

problems.prompt: Array vs linked list: which is better for frequent random access by index? For frequent insertion in the middle?
problems.answer: Random access: array (O(1) vs O(n)). Insertion in the middle once you hold the position: linked list (O(1) vs O(n) shifting).

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Queue = FIFO; circular arrays reuse space.
  • Linked list: O(1) insertion at a known place, O(n) search.
